security_spec.violation_condition: Linux kernel interrupt handler returns via ipopxret (generated by __attribute__((interrupt)) with Smip-aware compiler) after the kernel has modified the interrupted context's saved x10-x15 registers in pt_regs for signal delivery, ptrace register writes, or seccomp filter return-value rewriting; ipopxret restores x10-x15 from the hardware-private stack frame at implementation-defined offsets, silently discarding all kernel modifications to those registers
security_spec.summary: ipopxret restores x10-x15 from opaque hardware stack frame, silently undoing any kernel modifications to the interrupted context's argument registers

findings.finding: ret_from_exception uses explicit software register restore from pt_regs on the kernel stack (restore_from_x6_to_x31 at line 308 loads x10-x15 from PT_A0-PT_A5) followed by sret, NOT sipopret. All kernel modifications to pt_regs->a0 through pt_regs->a5 are correctly loaded back into hardware registers before returning to user mode. No __attribute__((interrupt)) is used anywhere in arch/riscv — the interrupt path is entirely hand-written assembly.
findings.snippet:
REG_L a0, PT_STATUS(sp)
csrw CSR_STATUS, a0
csrw CSR_EPC, a2
REG_L x1,  PT_RA(sp)
REG_L x3,  PT_GP(sp)
REG_L x4,  PT_TP(sp)
REG_L x5,  PT_T0(sp)
restore_from_x6_to_x31
REG_L x2,  PT_SP(sp)
sret

spec_citations.excerpt: sipopret: Restores registers x10-x15 from hardware-private stack frame at implementation-defined offsets, then executes sret. The order and access size of the loads, as well as the OFFSETS, are implementation-defined. Included in: Ssip.

When executing an xipopret instruction the context saved during the trap is restored and a return is executed. Actions in order: Conditionally performs stack pointer swap via xcspspop, Restores registers x10-x15, Adjust the stack pointer to destroy the stack frame, Executes an xret.

findings.finding: The interrupt/exception entry path explicitly saves all registers x1-x31 (including x10-x15 / a0-a5) to the pt_regs structure on the kernel stack via save_from_x6_to_x31 at line 167. This is a full software save — there is no ipush instruction or hardware-private stack frame. The Smip spec (aclic.adoc:1480) says that with Smip, registers x10-x15 are saved to a hardware-private stack frame at implementation-defined offsets, bypassing pt_regs. Since this kernel has no Smip support, the full software save to pt_regs is correct.
findings.snippet:
.Lsave_context:
    REG_S sp, TASK_TI_USER_SP(tp)
    REG_L sp, TASK_TI_KERNEL_SP(tp)
    addi sp, sp, -(PT_SIZE_ON_STACK)
    REG_S x1,  PT_RA(sp)
    REG_S x3,  PT_GP(sp)
    REG_S x5,  PT_T0(sp)
    save_from_x6_to_x31

spec_citations.excerpt: It performs the following operations in order: Save registers x10-x15, Adjusts the stack pointer to create the stack frame, Conditionally performs a stack pointer swap by executing xcspspush sp. NOTE: Intentionally, the GPRs are saved on the stack owned by the interrupted context.

findings.finding: Signal delivery modifies regs->a0, a1, a2 in pt_regs to set up signal handler calling convention. On a non-Smip system this is safe because ret_from_exception restores all registers from pt_regs via software loads before sret. However, this code is a documented risk point: if the kernel were ever compiled with Smip support (__attribute__((interrupt)) or sipopret in the return path), these pt_regs writes would be silently discarded by sipopret which restores x10-x15 from the hardware-private stack frame instead of from pt_regs. The signal handler would receive garbage in a0/a1/a2.
findings.snippet:
regs->a0 = ksig->sig;                     /* a0: signal number */
regs->a1 = (unsigned long)(&frame->info); /* a1: siginfo pointer */
regs->a2 = (unsigned long)(&frame->uc);   /* a2: ucontext pointer */

spec_citations.excerpt: sipopret: scspspop sp, sp; lr a0, OFFSET(sp); lr a1, OFFSET(sp); lr a2, OFFSET(sp); lr a3, OFFSET(sp); lr a4, OFFSET(sp); lr a5, OFFSET(sp); addi sp, sp, FRAMESIZE; sret. The order and access size of the loads, as well as the OFFSETS, are implementation-defined.

findings.finding: Same risk as setup_rt_frame: compat signal delivery writes a0/a1/a2 to pt_regs. On a Smip system using sipopret, these kernel modifications would be discarded because sipopret loads x10-x15 from the hardware-private stack frame at implementation-defined offsets, not from pt_regs.
findings.snippet:
regs->a0 = ksig->sig;                     /* a0: signal number */
regs->a1 = (unsigned long)(&frame->info); /* a1: siginfo pointer */
regs->a2 = (unsigned long)(&frame->uc);   /* a2: ucontext pointer */

findings.finding: Syscall restart logic writes regs->a0 (line 524: restart original a0; line 545: -EINTR on signal interruption) and regs->a7 (line 559: __NR_restart_syscall). All of these are in the x10-x15 range that sipopret restores from the hardware-private stack frame. On a Smip system, syscall restart and ERESTART* handling would be silently corrupted.

rt_sigreturn calls restore_sigcontext which does __copy_from_user(regs, &sc->sc_regs, ...) — copying the entire saved register set from userspace directly into pt_regs including a0-a5. On a Smip system using sipopret, the userspace-supplied a0-a5 values in pt_regs would be ignored by the hardware's own a0-a5 restore from the private stack frame. This would break sigreturn completely, potentially allowing the signal handler's register values to leak back to the interrupted context.

spec_citations.excerpt: It performs the following actions in order: Conditionally performs stack pointer swap by executing xcspspop sp, Restores registers x10-x15, Adjust the stack pointer to destroy the stack frame, Executes an xret according to the current level.

findings.finding: Ptrace GPR write via user_regset_copyin copies raw data from a ptrace caller directly into the target's pt_regs, including a0-a5. On a Smip system with sipopret, the debugger-written a0-a5 values would be discarded. The debugger (e.g., GDB) would see its register writes silently ignored.

syscall_set_return_value writes regs->a0. Called from seccomp (SECCOMP_RET_ERRNO, SECCOMP_RET_TRACE, seccomp notify continuation) and ptrace (syscall return value modification). On a Smip system, these modifications are discarded by sipopret.
syscall_set_arguments writes regs->a1 through regs->a5. Called when ptrace modifies syscall arguments. On a Smip system, all five argument register modifications would be discarded by sipopret.

Syscall entry writes regs->orig_a0 and sets regs->a0 = -ENOSYS. On a Smip system, the -ENOSYS placeholder would be discarded by sipopret, potentially causing the syscall to use whatever value was in a0 from the hardware-private stack frame. This could lead to incorrect syscall results.

syscall_handler writes regs->a0 = fn(regs) — setting the syscall return value. On a Smip system, this would be discarded by sipopret. The user process would always see the return value from the hardware-private stack frame (i.e., whatever a0 was before the syscall trap), making all syscall return values silently wrong.
syscall_rollback writes regs->a0 = regs->orig_a0. Called from seccomp SECCOMP_RET_TRAP path. On a Smip system, the rollback would be silently discarded.
